text: Polynomial through n points; evaluate at k.

Lagrange interpolation (拉格朗日插值): the unique polynomial of degree < n through n points (xi, yi) is f(x) = Σi yi · Πj≠i (x − xj)/(xi − xj). Each term is 1 at xi and 0 at every other xj. Evaluating at one k costs O(n²), or O(n) when the xi are 0, 1, …, n − 1 (prefix and suffix products).
Use it when an answer is known to be a polynomial in k of small degree (sums of powers 1d + … + kd have degree d + 1): compute it for d + 2 small k by brute force, then interpolate to a huge k.
Four points of a cubic, evaluated at k = 10 modulo 998244353 (P4781). Checked with exact fractions in Python.
Keep numerator and denominator separately and invert once per term: n inverses in total instead of n².
Smallest-leaf encoding; Cayley n^(n−2).

A Prüfer sequence (Prüfer 序列) encodes a labelled tree on n vertices as a list of n − 2 labels: repeatedly remove the smallest leaf and write down its neighbour. Decoding reverses it. The map is a bijection, so there are exactly nn−2 labelled trees (Cayley's formula).

A vertex appears in the sequence exactly (degree − 1) times. So the number of trees with given degrees d1, …, dn is (n − 2)! / Π (di − 1)! (树的计数 P2290). Both directions run in O(n) with a moving pointer to the smallest leaf (P6086).
parent (root n) 9 for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) deg[fa[i]]++; // number of children 10 vector<int> code; 11 int ptr = 1; 12 while (deg[ptr] != 0) ptr++; // smallest leaf 13 int leaf = ptr;

15 int f = fa[leaf]; 16 code.push_back(f); 17 if (--deg[f] == 0 && f < ptr) leaf = f; // the parent became a smaller leaf: use it now 18 else { ptr++; while (deg[ptr] != 0) ptr++; leaf = ptr; } // next smallest leaf
20 for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) cout << code[i] << " ";
22 return 0;

Tree: 1, 2, 3 hang on 4; then 4 – 5 – 6 – 7, rooted at 7. Removing smallest leaves writes 4, 4, 4, 5, 6 (checked in Python). The trick: when a removed leaf's parent becomes a leaf with a smaller label than the pointer, it is the next smallest leaf, so use it immediately.
With the root fixed at n (never removed), edges can be stored as parent pointers, which makes O(n) encoding a single pass.
Average fixed colourings; necklaces.

Burnside's lemma (Burnside 引理): the number of colourings that are different up to a group of symmetries = the average number of colourings fixed by each symmetry. For rotations of an n-bead necklace with m colours, rotation by k fixes mgcd(k, n) colourings: answer = (1/n) Σk mgcd(k, n).

Pólya (Pólya 定理) is the same count written with cycles: each symmetry fixes m(number of cycles) colourings. Grouping rotations by d = gcd(k, n) gives (1/n) Σd | n φ(n/d) md, fast even for n = 10⁹ (P4980).
rotations 28 if (d * d != n) ans = (ans + phi(d) % MOD * power(n, n / d)) % MOD;
30 cout << ans * power(n, MOD - 2) % MOD << "\n"; // divide by the n rotations
32 return 0;
Checked against the direct Burnside sum over all n rotations in Python. With reflections too (bracelets), add the n reflections' fixed counts and divide by 2n.
Dividing by n modulo a prime needs n not divisible by the prime; here n ≤ 10⁹ < MOD.
Laplacian minor determinant.

The matrix-tree theorem (矩阵树定理 , Kirchhoff): build the Laplacian L = D − A (degrees on the diagonal, −1 per edge off the diagonal, multi-edges counted). The number of spanning trees equals the determinant of L with any one row and the same column removed. Weighted edges give the sum over spanning trees of the product of weights.

The determinant is Gaussian elimination (进阶篇第22章), mod a prime with inverses or mod anything with row-Euclid. Directed versions count arborescences (out-trees / in-trees) using in- or out-degrees (P6178).
The first graph is checked by trying every set of n − 1 edges in Python; the complete graph K4 has 44−2 = 16 spanning trees (Cayley, 23.2).
小 Z 的房间(P4111) needs the determinant modulo a non-prime: use the row-Euclid elimination from 进阶篇第22章 instead of inverses.
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. Lagrange: f(k) = Σ yᵢ Π (k − xⱼ)/(xᵢ − xⱼ); O(n²), one inverse per term.
2. Polynomial of degree d: compute d + 1 values, interpolate to any k.
3. Prüfer: remove smallest leaf, write its neighbour; vertex appears deg − 1 times.
4. Cayley: n^(n−2) labelled trees; given degrees: (n−2)!/Π(dᵢ − 1)!.
5. Burnside: average of fixed colourings; rotation by k fixes m^gcd(k, n).
6. Pólya: (1/n) Σ_{d|n} φ(n/d) m^d for necklaces.
7. Matrix-tree: det of the Laplacian minus one row and column.
